The Cold War Begins

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 1: Explain why and how the Cold War between the United States and the Soviet Union developed after World War II.

Core Objective 2: Analyze the impact of American efforts to contain the Soviet Union and the growth of global communism during Truman’s presidency.

IN MY WORDS: In your own words, why did the United States and the Soviet Union become enemies after World War II, and what did the United States do about it?

Reading AWhy the Cold War Began

Its origins lay in the seemingly unavoidable ideological conflict between democratic capitalism and authoritarian communism.

Russia, after all, had been invaded by Germany twice in the first half of the twentieth century, and some 23 million people had died as a result. Soviet leaders were determined to keep firm control over neighboring nations, just as the United States had been doing for decades in Central and South America.

Word help: origins = beginnings · ideological = about beliefs and ideas · capitalism = private businesses compete for profit · authoritarian = ruled by a leader who allows no opposition

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 25, “Truman and the Cold War” (Origins of the Cold War).

Reading BAn “Iron Curtain” over Eastern Europe

On May 12, 1945, four days after victory in Europe, Winston Churchill asked Harry Truman: “What is to happen about [Eastern] Europe? An iron curtain is drawn down upon [the Russian] front. We do not know what is going on behind [it].”

Beginning in the spring of 1945 and continuing for the next two years, the Soviet Union installed “puppet” governments—officially independent regimes that in reality took their orders from Moscow—across Central and Eastern Europe. . . . Opponents were exiled, silenced, executed, or imprisoned.

Word help: iron curtain = Churchill’s name for the line that cut off Soviet-controlled Eastern Europe from the West · puppet governments = governments that look free but obey another country · exiled = forced to leave the country

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 25, “Truman and the Cold War” (Conflicts with the Soviets).

Reading CContainment and the Truman Doctrine

The best way for the United States to deal with such an ideological foe, Kennan advised, was not military confrontation. Instead, he called for patient, persistent, and firm “strategic” efforts to “contain” Soviet expansionism over the long term, without resorting to war.

In March 1947, President Truman responded to the crisis in the eastern Mediterranean by asking Congress for $400 million to assist Greece and Turkey. More important, the president announced what came to be known as the Truman Doctrine. . . . the United States must “support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.”

Word help: contain = keep from spreading · expansionism = trying to take more land or power · persistent = not giving up · doctrine = an official policy · subjugation = being forced under someone’s control

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 25, “The Containment Policy” (The Truman Doctrine) (p. 1117).

Reading DThe Marshall Plan, the Berlin Airlift, and NATO

From 1948 until 1951, the program provided $13 billion to sixteen European nations to revive their war-ravaged economies.

In June 1948, Stalin stopped all road, rail, and water traffic into West Berlin. . . . To provide West Berliners with desperately needed food and supplies, the United States and its allies organized a massive airlift of material into West Berlin. . . . The Berlin airlift went on for 321 days without any shots being fired.

The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), the largest defensive alliance in the world, declared that an attack against any of the members would be an attack against all. . . . By joining NATO, the United States committed itself to go to war on behalf of its allies.

Word help: Marshall Plan = the U.S. program to rebuild Europe · revive = bring back to life · traffic = cars, trains, and boats moving · airlift = carrying supplies in by airplane · alliance = a group of nations that promise to help each other

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 25, “The Containment Policy” (The Marshall Plan; The Berlin Blockade; Forming Alliances).

Map key: Yellow = French zone · Green = U.S. zone · Purple = British zone · Orange = Soviet zone · Dark blue line = the Iron Curtain · Access corridor = the path from West Germany to Berlin

Truman and the Fair Deal

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 3: Describe Truman’s efforts to expand the New Deal, and evaluate the effectiveness of his own Fair Deal agenda.

IN MY WORDS: What did Truman want to do at home, and how much of it did Congress let him do?

Reading EThe Baby Boom

Americans born in the two decades after 1945 composed what came to be called the baby boom generation, a disproportionately large group that would shape the nation’s social and cultural life throughout the second half of the twentieth century and after.

Word help: decades = periods of ten years · composed = made up · disproportionately = unusually

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 25, “Expanding the New Deal” (From War to Peace).

Reading FStrikes and the Taft-Hartley Act

In early 1947, the new Republican-controlled Congress sought to curb the power of unions by passing the Taft-Hartley Labor Act, which allowed employers to campaign against efforts to form unions.

Truman vetoed the Taft-Hartley Act, denouncing it as “bad for labor, bad for management, and bad for the country.” . . . Congress, however, overrode the president’s veto and Taft-Hartley became law, largely because southern Democrats overwhelmingly supported it.

Word help: strikes = workers refusing to work to win better pay · curb = limit · vetoed = rejected a bill · overrode = passed the law anyway with a two-thirds vote

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 25, “Expanding the New Deal” (Wages, Prices, and Labor Unrest; Political Cooperation and Conflict).

Reading GCivil Rights and the Dixiecrats

In July 1948, Truman issued an executive order banning racial segregation in the armed forces.

White delegates from Alabama and Mississippi walked out in protest. The solidly Democratic South had fractured over race. . . . On July 17, rebellious southern Democrats organized their own convention in Birmingham, Alabama. While waving Confederate flags and singing “Dixie,” they nominated South Carolina’s segregationist governor, Strom Thurmond, on a States’ Rights Democratic Party ticket. The press quickly dubbed them the Dixiecrats.

Word help: executive order = a rule the president makes · segregation = keeping races apart · delegates = party members at a convention · segregationist = someone who wants races kept apart · fractured = broke apart

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 25, “Expanding the New Deal” (Truman and Civil Rights; The Surprise Election of 1948).

Source 1To Secure These Rights, 1947 (Primary Source)

In 1946, President Truman created a committee to study civil rights in the United States. Its 1947 report, To Secure These Rights, became a plan for civil rights reforms. Here the committee looks at recent progress.

“Since the assignment of this Committee is to recommend ways of strengthening the civil rights of all of the people, we have naturally made it our business to consider the ways in which they are weak. . . . Mention should also be made of the ending of segregated schools in cities like Trenton and Gary . . . the establishment of interracial churches in many communities. . . . Since 1940, the annual figure has never exceeded 6; on the other hand, there has not yet been a year in which America has been completely free of the crime of lynching.”

Word help: assignment = job · segregated = separated by race · interracial = including people of different races · lynching = a murder by a mob, without a trial

To Secure These Rights: The Report of the President’s Committee on Civil Rights, 1947. In Norton, Ch. 25, “Another Red Scare,” Comparing Perspectives (p. 1146).

Source 1. Name two signs of progress the committee saw. Then name one problem it said was still not solved.

Point of view. Truman created this committee to recommend ways to strengthen civil rights. Why would the committee focus on “the ways in which they are weak” instead of only praising progress?

Picture 1“Dewey Defeats Truman” (1948)

Harry Truman holds up a newspaper the morning after the 1948 election. Norton’s caption: “Truman’s victory in 1948 was such a surprise that this early edition of the Chicago Daily Tribune reported (mistakenly) that Dewey had won.” (It is a primary source.)

What to look for: the headline = the big words at the top of the paper · Dewey = Thomas Dewey, the Republican candidate · Truman’s face = how he feels about the mistake

Norton, Ch. 25, “Expanding the New Deal” (The Surprise Election of 1948), photo “Dewey Defeats Truman.” Primary source.

Reading HA Surprise Win and the Fair Deal

The polls predicted a sure win for Thomas Dewey, but on Election Day Harry Truman pulled off the biggest upset ever, taking 24.2 million votes (49.5 percent) to Dewey’s 22 million (45.1 percent) and winning by a thumping margin of 303 to 189 in the Electoral College . . . Democrats also regained control of both houses of Congress.

The bipartisan conservative coalition rejected Fair Deal proposals such as several civil rights bills, national health insurance, federal aid to education, and a new approach to subsidizing farmers. . . . Yet the Fair Deal was not a complete failure. It laid the foundation for programs that the next generation of reformers would promote a decade later.

Word help: upset = a surprise win by the one expected to lose · Electoral College = the votes that actually choose the president · bipartisan = from both parties · coalition = a group working together

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 25, “Expanding the New Deal” (The Surprise Election of 1948; The Fair Deal Rejected).

Korea and the Red Scare

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 4: Assess the major international developments during the period 1949–1950, including the outbreak of the Korean War, and explain how U.S. foreign policy changed as a result.

Core Objective 5: Examine the emergence of the Red Scare and explain its impact on American politics and society.

IN MY WORDS: Name two events from 1949–1950 that made Americans more afraid of communism. How did that fear change life at home?

Reading IChina, the Bomb, and NSC-68

After World War II, the Communists won over most of the peasants. By the end of 1949, the Nationalist government was forced to flee to the island of Formosa, which it renamed Taiwan.

That the Soviets now possessed atomic weapons intensified every Cold War confrontation. . . . NSC-68 endorsed George Kennan’s containment strategy. But where Kennan had focused on political and economic counterpressure, the report called for a massive military buildup and “a policy of calculated and gradual coercion” against Soviet expansionism—everywhere.

Word help: peasants = poor farmers · possessed = had · intensified = made stronger · endorsed = supported · military buildup = making the army and weapons much bigger · coercion = using force or threats

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 25, “The Cold War Heats Up” (“Losing” China; The Soviets Develop Atomic Bombs; NSC-68) (p. 1135).

Reading JWar in Korea

On June 25, 1950, North Korean troops launched a coordinated attack across the 38th parallel . . . Within three days of fighting, the North Korean army had captured Seoul, the South Korean capital.

The Korean conflict was the first military action fought under the international flag of the United Nations, and some twenty other nations participated along with the United States. . . . Truman dodged the constitutional issue by officially calling the conflict in Korea a “police action” rather than a war.

Word help: 38th parallel = the line dividing North and South Korea · coordinated = carefully planned · United Nations = a world group of nations · constitutional issue = a question about the Constitution (it says only Congress can declare war) · dodged = avoided

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 25, “The Cold War Heats Up” (War Erupts).

Reading KMacArthur Fired, Korea Divided

On April 11, 1951, with civilian control of the military at stake, President Truman removed General MacArthur and replaced him with General Matthew B. Ridgway, who Truman felt better understood how to conduct a modern war in pursuit of limited objectives. . . . “I fired him because he wouldn’t respect the authority of the President.”

No peace treaty was ever signed, and Korea—like Germany—remained divided. . . . The war cost the United States more than 33,000 battle deaths and 103,000 wounded or missing.

Word help: civilian control = elected leaders, not generals, make the final decisions · limited objectives = small, specific goals, not total victory · battle deaths = soldiers killed in battle

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 25, “The Cold War Heats Up” (Sacking a Hero; A Cease-Fire) (p. 1140).

Reading LHUAC and the Hollywood Ten

Since 1938, the House Committee on Un-American Activities (HUAC) had claimed that Communist agents were infiltrating the federal government.

In May 1947, charges that the movie industry in Hollywood was a “hotbed of communism” led HUAC to launch a full-blown investigation. . . . Ten witnesses refused to answer questions about their political activities, arguing that such questions violated their First Amendment rights. . . . All ten were cited for contempt of Congress, imprisoned, and blacklisted (banned) from the film industry.

Word help: infiltrating = secretly getting inside · hotbed = a place full of something · First Amendment = the right to free speech · contempt of Congress = refusing to obey Congress · blacklisted = banned from work

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 25, “Another Red Scare” (The Hollywood Ten) (p. 1142).

Reading MMcCarthyism

He charged that the State Department had been infiltrated by Communists for years—and he claimed to have a list of their names, although he never provided it.

By the summer of 1951, what had come to be called McCarthyism had gotten out of control. . . . Though McCarthy failed to uncover even a single Communist agent in the federal government, his smear campaigns went largely unchallenged until the end of the Korean War. In the process, he tarnished many lives and reputations and created a chilling effect on free speech. Merely the accusation of Communist association was enough to ruin lives.

Word help: He = Senator Joseph McCarthy of Wisconsin · infiltrated = secretly entered · smear campaigns = attacks with false stories · tarnished = damaged · chilling effect = making people afraid to speak · accusation = a charge that someone did wrong

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 25, “Another Red Scare” (Joseph McCarthy’s Witch-Hunt).

Picture 2Senator Joseph McCarthy, 1954

Norton’s caption: “This 1954 photo shows McCarthy, the crusading senator who was determined to ‘sweep’ the Communists out of the federal government and beyond.” (It is a primary source.)

What to look for: the broom = a tool for sweeping out dirt · the dome behind him = the U.S. Capitol, where Congress meets · crusading = fighting hard for a cause

Norton, Ch. 25, “Another Red Scare” (Joseph McCarthy’s Witch-Hunt), photo “Joseph R. McCarthy,” 1954. Primary source.

Ike and the Affluent Society

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 6: Explain President Dwight Eisenhower’s political philosophy and domestic priorities.

Core Objective 7: Identify the factors that contributed to America’s postwar prosperity and analyze how that prosperity benefited women and people of color.

IN MY WORDS: What was Eisenhower’s “middle” approach at home? Why did so many Americans get richer in the 1950s, and who was left out?

Reading NModerate Republicanism

Committed to what he called moderate Republicanism, President Eisenhower promised to balance the federal budget, cut government spending, restore the authority of state and local governments, and restrain the federal government from engaging in the kind of political and social “engineering” represented by Franklin Roosevelt and the New Deal.

President Eisenhower labeled his domestic program “dynamic conservatism,” by which he meant being “conservative when it comes to money and liberal when it comes to human beings.” He kept intact the basic structure of the Democrats’ New Deal, even convincing Congress to establish a federal Department of Health, Education, and Welfare and to extend Social Security benefits to millions of workers formerly excluded: white-collar professionals, housekeepers and salesclerks, farmworkers, and members of the armed forces.

Word help: balance the budget = spend no more than the government takes in · restrain = hold back · domestic = at home, inside the country · formerly excluded = left out before

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 26, “Moderate Republicanism: The Eisenhower Years” (p. 1156). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 26, “Moderate Republicanism: The Eisenhower Years” (“Dynamic Conservatism” at Home) (p. 1158).

Reading OHighways and the Fall of McCarthy

The Federal-Aid Highway Act (1956) created a network of interstate highways modeled after the German autobahns (limited-access national highways) to serve the needs of commerce and defense as well as the public.

On December 2, 1954, the Senate voted 67–22 to “condemn” McCarthy for his reckless tactics. Soon thereafter, his political influence collapsed.

Word help: interstate = connecting the states · commerce = business and trade · condemn = officially blame · reckless = careless and dangerous

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 26, “Moderate Republicanism: The Eisenhower Years” (Transportation Improvements) (p. 1159). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 26, “Moderate Republicanism: The Eisenhower Years” (The Fall of McCarthy) (p. 1162).

Moderate Republicanism. Use Reading N. Eisenhower promised to cut spending, but did he get rid of the New Deal? Give one fact.

Reading PWhy the Economy Boomed: The GI Bill of Rights

Several factors led to the nation’s extraordinary prosperity. First, huge federal expenditures during World War II and the Korean War propelled the economy out of the Great Depression. . . . Military spending after 1945 represented 60 percent of the national budget and was by far the single most important stimulant to the economy.

Between 1944 and 1956, the GI Bill helped boost a huge number of poor and working-class Americans into the middle class. . . . Some 5 million veterans bought homes with the assistance of GI Bill mortgage loans, which required no down payment. Almost 8 million took advantage of GI Bill benefits to attend college or enroll in job-training programs.

Word help: extraordinary = unusual · expenditures = spending · propelled = pushed · middle class = families with steady jobs and enough money to live well · stimulant = something that speeds up growth · mortgage = a loan to buy a house

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 26, “A People of Plenty” (Postwar Prosperity) (p. 1163). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 26, “A People of Plenty” (The GI Bill of Rights) (p. 1165).

Reading QSuburbs, and Who Was Left Out

Yet racism restricted the benefits of the GI Bill for many Americans. . . . Even with GI Bill mortgage loans, Black veterans were often prevented from buying homes in White neighborhoods by the practice of “redlining,” whereby banks would refuse to provide mortgages to homebuyers based on their race or ethnicity.

Of the 13 million homes built between 1948 and 1958, more than 11 million were in the new suburbs. Americans—the great majority of whom were White—moved to the suburbs (“suburbia”) for a variety of reasons. . . . Levitt and other suburban developers created lily-White communities.

In 1950, women comprised 29 percent of the workforce, and that percentage rose steadily throughout the decade. . . . Women of color had even fewer vocational choices and were mostly delegated to low-paying domestic service jobs such as maids and cooks.

Word help: restricted = limited · redlining = banks refusing loans because of race · suburbs (suburbia) = neighborhoods outside cities · lily-White = only White people · vocational choices = job choices

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 26, “A People of Plenty” (The GI Bill of Rights; Suburban Culture; Shifting Women’s Roles).

Part 5 of 7

Critics and the Civil Rights Movement

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 8: Examine the major criticisms of postwar American society and consumer culture, and describe how they were expressed.

Core Objective 9: Evaluate the goals and major achievements of the civil rights movement during the 1950s.

IN MY WORDS: Who criticized 1950s America, and what did the civil rights movement win in the 1950s?

Reading RCracks in the Picture Window

In contrast to the “happy days” image of the 1950s, there was also widespread anxiety, dissent, and diversity. In The Affluent Society (1958), economist John Kenneth Galbraith attacked the prevailing notion that sustained economic growth would solve all major social problems.

Despite the historic growth of the middle class during the 1950s, chronic poverty remained amid America’s plenty. In 1959, one-fourth of the population had no financial assets, and more than half had no savings accounts or credit cards. Poverty afflicted nearly half the African American population, compared to one-fourth of Whites.

A small but highly influential group of writers, poets, painters, and musicians rejected the consumer culture and the traditional responsibilities of middle-class life. They were known as the Beats, a name that had a double meaning.

Word help: dissent = disagreement · prevailing = most common · chronic = lasting a long time · financial assets = money or property · consumer culture = a way of life built on buying things · the Beats = rebel writers and artists of the 1950s

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 26, “Cracks in the Picture Window” (Poverty amid Prosperity; The Beats) (p. 1173).

The critics. Give two ways critics said 1950s America was not as perfect as the “happy days” image.

Reading SBrown v. Board of Education (1954)

By the early 1950s, civil rights activists were challenging state laws requiring racial segregation in the public schools.

Warren himself wrote the groundbreaking opinion, delivered on May 17, 1954, that overturned the Plessy doctrine of “separate but equal.” The opinion cited a variety of sociological and psychological findings in ruling that even if racially separate schools were equal in quality, the very practice of separating students by race caused feelings of inferiority among Black children. A year later, the Court directed that racial integration should move forward “with all deliberate speed.”

Word help: segregation = keeping races apart · Warren = Earl Warren, chief justice of the Supreme Court · overturned = cancelled · inferiority = feeling less than others · integration = bringing races together

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 26, “The Early Years of the Civil Rights Movement” (The Brown Decision (1954)) (p. 1180).

Reading T“Massive Resistance”

In 1954, Harry F. Byrd, a Virginia senator and former governor, called for “massive resistance” against federal efforts to enforce integration in the South.

In 1956, more than 100 members of Congress signed a Declaration of Constitutional Principles (“Southern Manifesto”) deploring the Brown decision as “a clear abuse of judicial power” that had created an “explosive and dangerous condition” in the South. . . . By 1960, only 765 of 6,676 school districts in the South had desegregated.

Word help: massive resistance = all-out refusal to obey · enforce = make people obey · deploring = strongly criticizing · judicial = by the courts · desegregated = ended segregation

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 26, “The Early Years of the Civil Rights Movement” (“Massive Resistance”) (p. 1181).

Reading UThe Montgomery Bus Boycott

Less than three months after Emmett Till’s funeral in Chicago, in Montgomery, Alabama, on December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks, a forty-two-year-old African American seamstress, boarded the Cleveland Avenue bus and took a seat in the third row. As White passengers boarded, the White driver, James Blake, told Parks that she had to move to the back, as the city required Blacks to do. She refused.

The Montgomery bus boycott was a stunning success. For 381 days, African Americans, women and men, organized carpools, used Black-owned taxis, hitchhiked, or simply walked.

On December 20, 1956, the Montgomery boycotters won a federal case they had initiated against racial segregation on public buses. . . . They showed that well-coordinated, nonviolent Black activism could trigger major changes.

Word help: seamstress = a woman who sews for a living · boycott = refusing to use or buy something as a protest · initiated = started · trigger = cause

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 26, “The Early Years of the Civil Rights Movement” (The Montgomery Bus Boycott) (p. 1182).

Reading VKing, Nonviolence, and the SCLC

Combining the teachings of Mahatma Gandhi—the leader of the independence movement in India two decades earlier—with his own Christian tradition, King preached nonviolent civil disobedience, the tactic of defying unjust laws and peacefully suffering the consequences. Without confrontation, King believed, there would be no progress.

On January 10, 1957, King invited sixty Black ministers and leaders to Ebenezer Church in Atlanta. Their goal was to form an organization to promote nonviolent civil disobedience as a method of desegregating bus systems across the South. They established the Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC), with King as its president.

Word help: nonviolent civil disobedience = peacefully breaking unfair laws and accepting the punishment · defying = refusing to obey · confrontation = facing a problem head-on · desegregating = ending segregation in

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 26, “The Early Years of the Civil Rights Movement” (Martin Luther King Jr.; The Southern Christian Leadership Conference).

Part 6 of 7

Eisenhower’s Cold War

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 10: Explain how the Eisenhower administration’s commitment to “rolling back” communism around the world shaped U.S. foreign policy.

Core Objective 11: Assess the effectiveness of Eisenhower’s responses to the various foreign crises that arose during his presidency.

IN MY WORDS: How was Eisenhower’s plan for fighting communism different from Truman’s? Did his answers to world crises work?

Reading WRolling Back Communism: Massive Retaliation

The Truman administration’s commitment to containing communism focused on the Soviet threat to Western Europe. During the 1950s, the Eisenhower administration, especially Secretary of State John Foster Dulles, determined that containment was no longer enough; instead, the United States must develop a “dynamic” foreign policy that would “roll back” communism around the world.

So they crafted a strategy that came to be called “massive retaliation,” which meant using the threat of nuclear warfare to prevent Communist aggression. The strategy, they argued, would provide a “maximum deterrent at bearable cost,” or “more bang for the buck.”

The great weakness—and danger—of the massive retaliation strategy was that it escalated every global dispute into a possible war of annihilation.

Word help: roll back = push back and undo · retaliation = striking back · deterrent = something that stops an attack before it starts · annihilation = total destruction

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 26, “Foreign Policy in the 1950s” (p. 1187). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 26, “Foreign Policy in the 1950s” (Dulles and “Massive Retaliation”) (p. 1189).

Massive retaliation. What was “massive retaliation”? Why did Norton call it dangerous?

Reading XVietnam, Dien Bien Phu, and the Domino Theory

In December 1953, some 12,000 French soldiers parachuted into Dien Bien Phu, a cluster of villages in a valley ringed by mountains in northwestern Vietnam.

The president opposed U.S. intervention unless the British joined the effort. When they refused, Eisenhower told the French that U.S. military action was “politically impossible.” . . . On May 7, 1954, the Viet Minh fighters overwhelmed the last French resistance, marking the end of French colonial rule in Asia.

Eisenhower had used what he called the “falling-domino” theory to explain why the United States needed to fight communism in Vietnam: “You have a row of dominos set up, you knock over the first one, and what will happen to the last one is the certainty that it will go over very quickly.” If South Vietnam were to fall to communism, he predicted, the rest of Southeast Asia would soon follow.

Word help: Viet Minh = Vietnamese Communist fighters · intervention = getting involved · colonial rule = control by a foreign power · dominos = game tiles that knock each other over in a row

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 26, “Foreign Policy in the 1950s” (The Indochina War) (p. 1191–1192).

Reading YCrises in Hungary and at Suez (1956)

On October 23, 1956, Hungarian nationalists revolted against Communist troops. . . . They had been encouraged by American propaganda broadcasts through the Radio Free Europe network . . . Many Hungarians felt abandoned by the United States, having believed the U.S. propaganda that the leaders of the free world would support their rebellion.

Unable to retaliate directly against the United States, Nasser seized control of the Suez Canal Company and denied access to Israel-bound ships. . . . On November 5, British and French soldiers invaded the canal zone.

The president shocked Americans and much of the world by demanding that the British and French withdraw their troops from the Suez Canal and that the Israelis evacuate the Sinai Peninsula—or face severe economic sanctions. That the three aggressor nations grudgingly complied with a cease-fire agreement on November 7 testified to Eisenhower’s strength, influence, and savvy in dealing with military matters.

Word help: nationalists = people fighting for their nation’s freedom · propaganda = messages meant to persuade · retaliate = strike back · sanctions = penalties, like cutting off trade · complied = obeyed

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 26, “Reelection and Foreign Crises” (Repression in Hungary; The Suez War) (p. 1194–1196).
